profile.reading:
The facility identified here as PTC sits along 5th Street in Lyons, a small community in Linn County in Oregon's mid Willamette Valley. It is operated by Stayton Cooperative Telephone Company, commonly known as SCTC, a member owned rural telephone cooperative based in nearby Stayton. SCTC's own account of its history explains the name behind this facility's identifier. In 1997, the cooperative purchased People's Telephone Company, a small independent telephone exchange that had been serving the Lyons area, and folded its infrastructure into SCTC's broader network. The PTC in this facility's name almost certainly traces back to that acquired predecessor, People's Telephone Company, rather than to SCTC itself.

Rural telephone cooperatives like SCTC exist to provide voice, broadband, and related communications services to communities that are often too small or too sparsely populated to attract investment from the large national carriers. A building like this one typically functions as a central office or telephone exchange, housing switching equipment, fiber and copper distribution gear, and increasingly broadband and internet infrastructure, rather than serving as a commercial colocation data center marketed to outside tenants. That distinction matters for understanding its scale and purpose. It exists to serve SCTC's own local subscriber base in and around Lyons, not to house third party servers for hire.

SCTC does not publish square footage, power capacity, cooling design, or any other data center grade specification for this specific location on its own website, and no independent public record reviewed here fills that gap either. That absence of detail is unsurprising and, in its own way, informative. Facilities like this are typically small utility buildings sized to the equipment needs of a limited local subscriber base, built and expanded incrementally over decades rather than constructed as a single large capital project with an accompanying press release. Small rural cooperatives generally have neither the commercial incentive nor the practical need to publish the kind of technical marketing material that a colocation provider would use to attract enterprise tenants.

What the public record does establish is straightforward. This is a telephone cooperative facility in a small Willamette Valley town, operated by SCTC as part of its member owned communications network, with roots tracing back to a 1997 acquisition of a smaller local predecessor carrier. Beyond its location and its operator's identity, no further technical detail about the building itself is publicly available.

reading.body:
Stayton Cooperative Telephone Company is a rural telephone cooperative, not a data center operator, and its one recorded facility is a small exchange building in Lyons, Oregon with no published power or floor area.

The pattern here is a registry entry that looks like a data center and is not one. SCTC was incorporated in 1955 by consolidating eighteen Oregon telephone companies, and it bought People's Telephone Company of Lyons in 1997, which is the likely source of the PTC label on the building. The facility on 5th Street is switching and transport plant for the cooperative's own subscribers in the Santiam Canyon, the kind of building that houses equipment for a limited local base rather than servers for hire.

That distinction matters for anyone counting AI capacity. A rural exchange carries no critical IT load, no redundancy specification, and no leasable hall, so it contributes nothing to the compute supply that AI scaling depends on. The cooperative's own history, from mobile telephone service in 1976 to fiber to the home starting in 2007, describes a communications utility serving its members, not a landlord for third party compute.

What the data does not establish is the building's actual size, power draw, or equipment. SCTC publishes no floor area and no power figure, and the PTC abbreviation is recorded as likely rather than confirmed. The zero megawatts and zero square feet in the record are absences of published data, not measurements, so they should not be read as a finding about the site itself.
